title: Waraqa's warning
hookLine: Waraqa says the same angel came to Musa, and that his people would drive him out (Bukhari)

cards: Good news and bad news, from the same old man, in the same breath. Khadijah has brought her husband to her cousin, Waraqa ibn Nawfal, a learned man, old by now and blind. He listens to the whole account of the cave.
Then he tells the Prophet two things: a recognition, and a warning the Prophet doesn't expect. Today: Waraqa's warning.

teach.h: THIS IS THE NAMUS OF MUSA.
teach.b: The account is in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by 'Aishah. She says Waraqa had become a Christian before Islam, and that he wrote, and had copied from the Gospel as much as Allah willed.
First he says: this is the Namus, the one Allah sent down to Musa. It is understood as the angel Jibril. Then the warning: I wish I were young.
I wish I could be alive when your people drive you out. And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ asks, in the Arabic, a-wa mukhrijiyya hum?

teach.h: WILL THEY REALLY DRIVE ME OUT?
teach.b: Will they really drive me out? You can hear the surprise.
This is the man Mecca called al-Amin, the trustworthy, the one the clans chose to settle the stone.

teach.h: IF I LIVE, I'M WITH YOU.
teach.b: Waraqa's answer is plain: no man has ever come with anything like what you've brought without being treated as an enemy.
And if your day reaches me, I will help you with all my strength. A hard truth, told kindly, by someone who puts himself beside it: if I'm there, I'm with you. The warning did come true.
The Qur'an, years later, speaks of the time when those who disbelieved drove him out, and of Allah's help to him in the cave. But Waraqa didn't see it.
The hadith ends: not long after, Waraqa died, and the revelation paused.

how: Muslims remember Waraqa ibn Nawfal with respect as the learned cousin of Khadijah who recognized the revelation, and his warning is retold when the beginning of the Prophet's ﷺ mission is taught.

o: his people would drive him out, said by an old cousin
a curse an uncle shouted from the crowd at Safa
a dream that warned Khadijah of trouble ahead

s: Waraqa told him only good news
he recognized the angel, then warned: your people will drive you out.
Waraqa lived to see the Prophet leave Mecca
the hadith says he died not long after.
the Prophet was surprised by the warning
he asked: will they really drive me out?

games.q: you're Waraqa. you believe this young man will be driven out by his own people. he's already shaken. what do you tell him?
o: only the good part, to spare him.
the truth, and that you'll stand with him.
nothing, since you're old and can't help.
games.why: Waraqa told him plainly: no one brought this without being treated as an enemy. and then: if your day reaches me, I'll help you with all my strength.

practice: Think of something true you've been told and haven't wanted to hear, about your health, your work, a relationship, a habit, and let your own 'will they really?' be there without pushing it away.
Then think of who told you, and whether, like Waraqa, they stood beside you when they said it; if you pray, ask for the strength to take it in.

wordCard.voice: Waraqa's warning. Khadijah's old cousin recognized the angel who came to Musa, and told the Prophet his own people would drive him out, and promised to stand with him. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: 'will they drive me out?', the Prophet's question to Waraqa.

carryVoice: Your line: they will drive you out. A hard truth, and a friend standing beside it. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3 (Waraqa a Christian who copied from the Gospel; the Namus sent to Musa; 'will they drive me out?'; Waraqa's promise; his death and the pause)
Qur'an 9:40 (when those who disbelieved drove him out; Allah's help in the cave)
